newsitem.title: CHINA: ASIAN DEBT MARKETS - Currency jitters scupper FRN.
newsitem.headline: ASIAN DEBT MARKETS - Currency jitters scupper FRN.

text.p: Currency volatility has claimed another victim in Asian debt markets, with a floating-rate note (FRN) postponed because of high interest rates caused by the volatility.
Indonesian department store operator PT Matahari Putra Prima is postponing its five-year US$100 million FRN, bankers close to the deal confirmed on Tuesday.

"People are loath to issue in a market place where there's so much uncertainty, and the uncertainty ends up meaning that you end up getting priced above where you would in a normal market," one of the bankers said.
Bankers PT Matahari Putra Prima would return when market conditions improved.
They said Matahari did not have immediate need of the cash, so it could afford to wait rather than pay the premium imposed by investors alarmed at recent Asian currency volatility.
While no pricing details were confirmed, market talk was of a coupon of 210 basis points over the six-month London interbank offered rate (LIBOR).
The deal was being arranged by BT Asia and Bear Stearns Asia, and had no put or call options.
The wave of currency selling has hit the Indonesian rupiah, the Thai baht, the Malaysian ringgit and Philippine peso.
Since selling started in July, the baht has fallen more than 30 percent, the rupiah more than 20 percent, the ringgit more than 10 percent and the peso about 14 percent.
China, whose currency is not convertible, has had no problems in international debt markets, and one of its oldest joint venture banks will launch an issue on Wednesday.

Xiamen International Bank, the first Sino-foreign joint venture bank set up in China, will launch a US$40 million five year floating rate certificates of deposit (FRCD) issue on Wednesday, bankers said.
Arrangers are Development Bank of Singapore, Banque Nationale de Paris's Hongkong branch, Oversea-Chinese Banking Corp and DKB Asia.
The issue has a put option on the third anniversary.
Despite its strong foreign exchange reserves, Hong Kong has also been hit by currency jitters.

The Hong Kong government revealed recently it had spent US$1 billion defending the Hong Kong dollar and the Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA) on Monday warned banks in Hong Kong against speculating on the Hong Kong dollar.
The warning prompted banks to move to square their positions early on Tuesday, pushing overnight rates up to 20 percent in the morning session.
